title: Germany: Russia’s Enemy No. 1
content:
Russia has targeted many European countries in its new shadow war offensive this summer. But Enemy No. 1 is Germany, the nation that has done more than any other to fund Ukraine and rebuild Europe’s crumbling defenses.

Infrastructure sabotage, assassination plots, drone incursions and the menacing of undersea cables have become commonplace. There are signals that this may be as serious as that of last fall. Or worse.

It’s not hard to see why the Kremlin targets Germany. The country increasingly acts as the linchpin of a hawkish but fledgling North European alliance determined to confront Russian aggression. Other countries in this grouping (the Nordic-Baltic eight, plus Poland) are also targeted, along with Romania, while most NATO members in Southern Europe are less affected.

Germany has faced several hybrid attacks in recent months. The key event was the discovery on August 4 of explosive-laden drones at Leipzig/Halle airport in eastern Germany, causing the shutdown of all its runways. Leipzig/Halle hosts Antonov Airlines, a Ukrainian cargo carrier that has four planes at the airport.

title: Armenia Battles to Buy Time
content:
Armenia wants to escape Russia’s embrace and knows how to achieve this. The Kremlin also knows this. The game now being played between the two will determine whether it succeeds in building new relationships or remains within Putin’s orbit.

The tug-of-war became serious after Armenia’s Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan was re-elected in June and has become fiercer since he announced plans to apply for EU membership. The idea is that the years-long process will ultimately raise Armenian prosperity and security. The problem is that in the meantime, the country’s foreign trade is deeply entwined with Russia.

Recognizing Yerevan’s dilemma, the Russian President has publicly pressed Nikol Pashinyan to make a rapid choice between the European Union and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) by holding a referendum. Moscow argues the two blocs are incompatible, while realizing that its influence is only likely to decline (trade dropped steeply in the first half of this year).

title: Kremlin Prepares to Cross the Final Red Line
content:
After the first wave of compulsory mobilization in 2022 brought broad opposition and an exodus of young men, the Russian authorities did their homework. As a result, they are significantly better prepared for the next round, which many observers expect may follow the September 18-20 Duma elections.

But surveys carried out by the Kyiv-based Institute for Conflict Studies and Analysis of Russia show opposition is not just high, it is also increasing.

Many Russians are deeply unhappy at the idea, and Putin’s inner circle, despite its tight control of information and communications, will have to take their opposition into account. Finding ways out of the country for their fighting age children has become an urgent talking point among middle class Russians in Moscow and St Petersburg.

Negative attitudes to compulsory mobilization became entrenched after the first wave, in the fall of 2022, and the share of Russians opposed to a repeat has remained at around three-quarters of the population since early 2024.

title: Frontline Arctic: The Evolution of Russia’s Military Posture in a Changing Arctic
content:
• Russia’s military posture and regional threat perception are steadfast. They relate to imposing cost on the access of foreign military assets to the Arctic Zone of the Russian Federation (AZRF) and through the Northern Sea Route (NSR); ensuring defense in depth by expanding interdiction capabilities beyond the AZRF; and protecting the NSR from perceived foreign encroachment against its disputable status as a “body of internal waters”.
  • Despite unchanging strategic priorities, the Kremlin has been compelled to adapt its military, defense, and security approach toward the region. These changes are compounded by over a decade of war against Ukraine, international isolation, sanctions, and the accelerating impacts of climate change. Russian authorities are vindicated but more vulnerable in the Arctic, a region where Moscow once held strategic dominance.
  • Moscow feels that both its control and sovereignty over the Arctic are slipping away. Russia is feeling increasingly vulnerable in the Arctic, especially in the context of Sweden and Finland joining NATO. Conventional limitations amplify the Kremlin’s increasing sense of vulnerability, particularly in the European High North.

title: Copycat Tech: Why the AI Bubble Might Burst
content:
Large language models share an open secret: they’re trained on the same data and generally detect the same patterns. Engineers race to produce updated versions only for their competitors to catch up to them within a few weeks. This makes for high production costs but low switching costs for customers.

It also makes for a fragile business model. 

This logic explains why many fear a bubble. A site called isaiprofitable.com adds up major AI companies’ announced revenue and subtracts expenditure — and comes up with a large negative number. AI companies have excited us with promises of revenue, overlooking whether those exceed the cost of producing them. Policymakers, in Europe and elsewhere, should be wary of pouring public money into gigafactories or other schemes to build copycat large language models just as investors are beginning to question the likelihood of them making profits. 

When ChatGPT 3.5 came out, OpenAI’s strategy looked like a classic three-stage capital expenditure play:

  • Build up a monopoly too expensive to replicate. 
  • Raise prices. 
  • Profit.

title: Armenia’s Relations With Russia? Worsening
content:
If you want one example of Armenia’s problems in shaking itself free of Russia’s influence, look at its rail system. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has repeatedly called for Russia to show flexibility and potentially transfer the concession to a third country acceptable to both sides. On 24 August, he again urged Russia to sell its concession rights to a mutually acceptable third party.

Russia has not answered, and it is unlikely to accept the idea. It has been running an escalating campaign to make life hard for Pashinyan, who was reelected in June. Putin makes no secret of this; indeed, he seems to delight in the (considerable) influence he can bring to bear.

That was clear at the September 1 meeting between the Russian and Armenian leaders at Bishkek, on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit. The reason is Armenia’s pursuit of closer ties with the European Union.

Putin sees this as a threat, as he once did with Ukraine. The EU’s anti-corruption, free trade, liberal democratic ethos is the antithesis of Russia’s approach.

title: CEPA Podcast: General (Ret.) Daniel Petrescu on What is Next for the NATO Alliance
content:
The CEPA Podcast is a series of dynamic interviews, bringing together leaders and experts from both sides of the Atlantic to explore the most important challenges shaping our world today. 

In this episode, General (Ret.) Daniel Petrescu, Romania’s former Chief of the Defence Staff, joins to explore where NATO goes after this year’s summit in Ankara. Drawing on Romania’s experience intercepting Russian drones out of its own airspace, he argues the alliance’s real potential lies in how fast allies can field and integrate new capabilities to face today’s threats. Petrescu makes the case for how a stronger Romania can bolster the alliance and why the Black Sea deserves more attention as a region for NATO’s leadership. 

Speakers:  

  • Gen. (Ret.) Daniel Petrescu, Member, International Leadership Council, Center for European Policy Analysis; Chief of the Defence Staff, Romanian Armed Forces (2019-2023) 

    • Moderated by: 

  • Kari Odermann, Fellow, Center for European Policy Analysis

    Click here to listen now. For questions regarding this episode, please contact Press@cepa.org

title: Dangerous Partners: The Russia-China Military Embrace
content:
Moscow and Beijing have not built a joint military space command, and they do not need one. Selective cooperation in missile warning, navigation, air and missile defense, and potentially counterspace operations is already making both countries harder to deter and US space power more vulnerable.

There is no evidence of a combined Russian-Chinese space command, no confirmed joint anti-satellite force, no integrated missile-warning network comparable to NORAD, and no known arrangement under which an attack on one country’s space assets would oblige the other to respond. Yet Moscow and Beijing are increasingly cooperating precisely in areas where limited coordination can produce disproportionate strategic effects.

Their relationship is best understood not as an emerging military alliance, but as selective strategic integration. Using this approach, they increasingly exchange technology, operational experience, infrastructure, and strategic concepts designed to reduce US military advantages.

Their joint exercises have so far displayed limited interoperability, but even modest coordination can complicate US and NATO defense planning.

title: NATO Must Match Russia’s Long-Range Missile Arsenal
content:
On the sidelines of this summer’s NATO Summit in Ankara, 12 allies, led by the UK, commited $50bn to developing deep strike precision capabilities. Then, in August, the new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced Ukraine would be given blueprints for long-range Storm Shadow cruise missiles.

These steps were welcome, but without further action they will not fill the long-range fire gap with Russia. Many of the new capabilities planned by the European group will not be available until the next decade.

European NATO not only lacks the integrated air and missile defense equipment to counter Russia’s long-range capabilities, but don’t have enough equally powerful missiles to deter the Kremlin.

Allied states and Ukraine need to come together to develop a strategy to remove the disparity in long-range weapons, especially as the alliance confronts production and cost issues around air defense systems and shortfalls in missile deliveries.

The Kremlin has invested heavily in an array of long-range weapons systems since 2018, including the Avangard, the Iksander, and the still experimental Burevestnik, giving it a dynamic range of capabilities, some of which are hypersonic.

title: AI’s Rubberstamp
content:
It’s the latest tech challenge: identify when students, authors, and others depend on AI to produce content. Anthropic places invisible statistical watermarks in Claude-generated text. Google deploys a similar technique, SynthID, in Gemini. OpenAI is testing watermarking ChatGPT responses. 

Under Europe’s Artificial Intelligence Act, new labeling rules took effect this summer. Companies must now mark AI-generated content and deepfakes that relate to public interest topics, including politics, public health, security, and the economy. The only exception is for content that has undergone genuine human review or editorial control.

While the US has no federal requirement to watermark AI-generated content, Congress has considered legislation, and several states have acted. California’s AI Transparency Act requires large providers to offer detection tools and embed origin disclosures in AI-generated images, video, and audio, though not text.

title: On a Train Under Russian Attack
content:
At 3:45 in the morning on September 13, a Ukrainian railway official woke me with one urgent Ukrainian word: Evacuatia.

I was on a train from Kyiv to Poland. There was no time to dress, so I joined the stream of passengers pouring out of the train in my cotton nightgown and slippers.

It was pitch black.

It wasn’t enough to be off the train. We needed distance from the carriages to be safe from drone shrapnel. The ground was uneven, and I held onto the arm of a tall man because, under the circumstances, falling seemed an especially bad idea.

I’m 85, and this was my seventh reporting trip to Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion. I’ve been in places where the air-raid sirens sound so often that people barely look up. I’ve interviewed torture survivors, amputees and children whose education is repeatedly interrupted by races to bomb shelters.

Still, until Sunday morning, I had never had to run from a Russian drone myself. The alarm was well-judged: we soon heard the thud of an explosion and later learned that it had hit the railroad track behind us. One passenger, a former member of the CIA, estimated that it was between 100 and 200 meters away.
snippet: At 3:45 in the morning on September 13, a Ukrainian railway official woke me with one urgent Ukrainian word: Evacuatia.
creator: Sara George

title: German Car Crisis: A Defense Bonanza?
content:
Volkswagen, the world’s second-largest auto manufacturer, is slashing 100,000 jobs. Auto suppliers Bosch and ZF are cutting tens of thousands more, putting at risk a combined 350,000 jobs across the continent. 

But behind the grim news, there’s hope: Europe’s struggling automakers are diversifying into defense manufacturing. Israel’s Rafael signed a letter of intent to take over Volkswagen’s 2,300-worker Osnabrück factory. It plans to build Iron Dome launchers, generators and trucks. Renault has cleared a 5,000-square-meter hall to assemble Chorus strike drones. Auto supplier Schaeffler is selling electronics parts to German drone maker Helsing. 

Europe’s defense and car industries make natural partners. They require similar skills. One is growing. The other is declining, bloodied by Chinese competition and the transition to electric vehicles. By working together, the two can offset the pain and increase the continent’s security — provided they can overcome several obstacles.
